newsitem.title: USA: Hilton files proxy for control of ITT's board.
newsitem.headline: Hilton files proxy for control of ITT's board.

text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp. filed its proxy statement on Monday asking ITT Corp. shareholders to replace ITT's board of directors with a Hilton-nominated slate that would support its $6.5 billion hostile bid for ITT.
The proxy solicitation would give Hilton's management the ability to vote in place of ITT shareholders at ITT's next annual meeting.

Hilton, the nation's largest hotel and gambling company, would then elect 11 new members to replace ITT's current board. Fourteen additional nominees were put on the slate in case ITT increases the number of board members before the annual meeting.
These directors "are expected ... to remove obstacles to the consummation of the offer and the proposed Hilton merger," the Beverly Hills, Calif.-hotel and gambling company said in its filing.

Hilton also asked for votes on one measure urging ITT management to sell the company to Hilton and on a second provision to repeal any changes to ITT's corporate bylaws since last being revised on July 23. This second provision would restrict ITT from adopting some defence strategies.
ITT spokesman Jim Gallagher had no reaction to Hilton's proxy filing, which had been expected.
He said ITT, owner of the Sheraton hotel chain and Caesars World Casinos, has yet to schedule an annual meeting, and he gave no indication when that might happen.

Last year, ITT's annual meeting was held on May 14. By law in Nevada, where it is incorporated, ITT must call an annual meeting within 18 months after the previous one, meaning ITT must hold an annual meeting in mid-November at the latest.
In the filing, Hilton also said a combined company would be run by Hilton's management. It did not mention roles for ITT Chairman Rand Araskog or other ITT executives.

Marc Grossman, senior vice president of corporate affairs at Hilton, on Monday reiterated earlier statements that Hilton was still open to carving out a role for Araskog and the others "if the two companies could talk."
But so far, New York-based ITT has been unwilling to discuss the proposed deal.

Within 10 days of the original offer, ITT rejected it as "inadequate" and launched a defensive effort to sell assets and refocus on core businesses in hotels and gambling -- the very units Hilton wants to own.

In a letter to Araskog delivered on Monday, Hilton Chief Executive Officer Stephen Bollenbach again asked for meetings with ITT. He noted Marriott International Inc.'s $1 billion acquisition of Renaissance Hotel Group as a sign that "our competitors will not stand still."
He also said "a true focus on your core businesses involves more than simply selling non-strategic assets."
Hilton's initial $55 per share tender offer expires on Feb. 28, but it is likely Hilton will extend the terms.
Grossman said the company will decide whether to extend the deal as the date looms nearer. He said some shares have been tendered, but declined to give an amount.

Financial analysts believe an extended battle over the future of ITT lies ahead because Hilton's initial offer is too low. The consensus on Wall Street calls for a more likely sale price at around $65 a share.

Next up for the companies is a March 5 hearing in federal Court in Las Vegas over a Hilton lawsuit seeking to bar ITT from changing its board membership or using its "poison pill" defence as a means of thwarting Hilton's bid.
Hilton shares fell 25 cents to $25.875, while ITT rose 25 cents to $57.75 a share on the New York Stock Exchange.
